I've always considered myself a libertarian and have called myself one since I was about 15. Over the years I have had to modify what I called myself to green libertarian. It has become clear to me that individuals and private enterprises would suck at managing the environment. To maintain biodiversity, large enough areas to allow for natural migratory patterns, and of course pollution, does require an organization that can think on a larger scale and longer term then what a true libertarian society could accomplish. I'm not saying our current government is the answer or that they are even do a good job at it now. I'm just saying the selfishness and money first attitude of the human race as it is now would be a disaster if left manage the environment in a truly libertarian government.

You're discounting individual self-interest in seeing tracts preserved.

As one example, a fellow named Jay B. Starkey, a Florida cattle rancher, set aside an 18,000 acre region (about 21 square miles) as a wilderness preserve in central Florida, now called the Starkey Wilderness Preseve. In the absence of government, there's no reason that he couldn't have left that land to an non-profit organization whose charter is designed for the same purpose.

The fact is, some individuals have an interest in preserving the environment. Take yourself as evidence. And a percentage of individuals who have the wealth and resources also feel the same way, and would take steps to see that vision carried out with or without a government to do the work.

While your notion is agreeable on the face of it, deeper inspection shows it to be bankrupt.

What are the relative numbers that are for each side, and what is the relative purchasing power of each side? It seems to me that for every Jay B. Starkey there are hundreds who don't care about the environment. I feel that the argument comes down to whether you want the government to enforce a morality that most likely does not align with the desires of the majority of the people (or the majority of the money) for the betterment of the ecosystem we inhabit for future generations.

Obviously if everyone thinks like that it wouldn't be a problem, but opinions like this come down to how we are educated and what we value because of that education. Now you might say that this is easily resolved because people will choose to send their kids to the best place to educate them so of course they will learn to think critically for themselves, but this only means that they will choose the place that they perceive as the best not necessarily the one that is. I point to Apple as evidence. It is marketed as the best and people buy it and think it is because of the brand and their perception of what it represents, even though it factually isn't the best product on the market.

I hold libertarian ideas in high regard, but there are somethings that I think the government must handle. I think a lot of people are too stupid to allow it to work in its pure form. I apologize for lack of citations, but hopefully this doesn't invalidate my point.
